questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has a 2 day history of an aching red left eye. Bright light makes it much worse. Her vision is slightly blurred. There is redness concentrated in a ring around the cornea, and the left pupil is smaller than the right and slightly irregular. There is no discharge. Her temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pain, photophobia, ciliary (circumcorneal) flush and a small irregular pupil is anterior uveitis (iritis), the commonest form of uveitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: smaller than the right and slightly irregular
Bright light makes it much worse
steps.x: **Ciliary flush** + **photophobia** + **small irregular pupil** = iritis.

elim: Gives a fixed mid-dilated pupil and hazy cornea, not a small pupil.
Gives discharge with diffuse redness and normal pupil and vision.
Segmental redness, mild discomfort, no photophobia or pupil change.
Painless red patch with normal vision.

steps.x: **B. Anterior uveitis.** Small pupil = uveitis; mid-dilated fixed pupil = acute glaucoma.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has a painful red right eye with photophobia for 1 day. He has had 18 months of low back pain that wakes him in the second half of the night and improves with exercise. Lumbar flexion is reduced. There is ciliary flush around the right cornea.
questions.q: Which underlying condition is most likely?
questions.e: Inflammatory back pain with acute anterior uveitis in a young man is ankylosing spondylitis, the condition most strongly associated with uveitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which underlying condition is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: wakes him in the second half of the night
steps.x: Inflammatory back pain + iritis = **ankylosing spondylitis** (HLA-B27).

elim: Needs recurrent oral and genital ulcers; usually bilateral panuveitis.
Improves with rest, not exercise, and has no eye link.
Peripheral small joints; linked to scleritis rather than iritis.
Gives cough, hilar nodes and erythema nodosum, not inflammatory back pain.

steps.x: **A. Ankylosing spondylitis.** Uveitis is strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has a painful red left eye with photophobia and blurred vision. Four weeks ago he had urethral discharge after unprotected sex. He now has a swollen right knee and pain at the back of his heel. Slit-lamp examination shows cells in the anterior chamber.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Anterior uveitis secondary to reactive arthritis
questions.e: Urethritis followed by asymmetrical lower limb arthritis and enthesitis is reactive arthritis, which is associated with anterior uveitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Infection then **knee + heel** + red eye = reactive arthritis with iritis.

elim: Gives a corneal opacity, not anterior chamber cells with arthritis.
Gives profuse purulent discharge, not anterior chamber cells.
Different age and joint pattern; no anterior chamber cells as the key sign.
He is not septic; this is a sterile post-infective picture.

steps.x: **A. Anterior uveitis secondary to reactive arthritis.** Uveitis associations: AS, reactive arthritis, sarcoidosis, IBD.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has a 2 week history of increasingly blurred vision in her right eye with many floating dark spots. Her eye is not red or painful. Visual acuity is 6/24. Dilated fundoscopy shows a hazy vitreous with patches of inflammation in the choroid and retina.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gradually worsening blurred vision over days with floaters and choroidal inflammation in a white quiet eye is posterior uveitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Floaters + blur over days + **choroid** involved = posterior uveitis.

elim: Gives a painful red photophobic eye with ciliary flush.
Sudden painless loss with a cherry red spot, not over 2 weeks with vitritis.
Sudden floaters and flashes without choroidal inflammation.
Central distortion in older patients with no vitritis.

steps.x: **C. Posterior uveitis.** Posterior uveitis: painless floaters and blurred vision worsening over days.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man of Turkish origin has blurred vision in both eyes and floaters for 1 week. He has had recurrent painful mouth ulcers for years and two episodes of painful genital ulcers. A small red pustule formed at a recent blood test site. Both fundi show retinal vasculitis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Bilateral uveitis due to Behçet's disease
questions.e: Recurrent oral and genital ulcers, pathergy and bilateral uveitis with retinal vasculitis are characteristic of Behçet's disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: red pustule formed at a recent blood test site
steps.x: Oral + genital ulcers + **pathergy** + bilateral eye disease = **Behçet's**.

elim: No ulcers or pathergy; would expect cough and hilar nodes.
No diabetes; not inflammatory.
Unilateral dendritic corneal ulcer.
No preceding infection or arthritis; does not cause pathergy.

steps.x: **A. Bilateral uveitis due to Behçet's disease.** Bilateral uveitis with systemic disease is characteristic of Behçet's.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has had several attacks of iritis in his left eye. Today the eye is painful again. When dilating drops are given, the left pupil dilates into a flower-like, irregular shape because parts of the iris margin remain stuck down.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding causing the irregular pupil?
questions.e: Posterior synechiae are adhesions of the inflamed iris to the anterior lens capsule, giving an irregular pupil on dilation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding causing the irregular pupil? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Iris stuck to the lens after iritis = **posterior synechiae**.

elim: Iris adheres to the cornea at the angle, not to the lens.
Gives a small regular pupil with ptosis.
A congenital keyhole defect.
An optic nerve sign, not a shape abnormality.

steps.x: **D. Posterior synechiae.** Complications of uveitis: vision loss, posterior synechiae, cataract, glaucoma.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with recurrent anterior uveitis has used prednisolone acetate drops on and off for 6 years. She now complains of gradually increasing glare from car headlights at night and blurred vision in that eye. The eye is white and quiet today. The red reflex is dull.
questions.q: Which complication is most likely?
questions.e: Chronic inflammation and long-term steroid use both cause cataract, which gives glare and a dull red reflex.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which complication is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: prednisolone acetate drops on and off for 6 years
steps.x: Glare + dull red reflex after years of steroid drops = **cataract**.

elim: Would cause pain and redness with fluorescein staining.
Sudden floaters and flashes, normal red reflex.
Gives a curtain over vision, not gradual glare.
Inherited night blindness with tunnel vision from childhood.

steps.x: **A. Cataract.** Chronic uveitis and steroid drops cause cataract and raised IOP.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with recurrent iritis has severe left eye pain, headache and vomiting. The eye is red, the cornea is hazy and the pupil is stuck down to the lens around its whole margin. The iris is bowed forward. Intraocular pressure is 52 mmHg (10–21).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his raised intraocular pressure?
o: Secondary angle-closure glaucoma from posterior synechiae
questions.e: 360° posterior synechiae trap aqueous behind the iris (iris bombé), pushing it forward to close the angle: secondary angle-closure glaucoma.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his raised intraocular pressure? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: stuck down to the lens around its whole margin
steps.x: Iris glued to the lens all round = aqueous trapped = **iris bombé** = angle closes.

elim: Pressure is not normal; it is very high.
Causes open-angle glaucoma in young myopes, not iris bombé.
Gradual and painless, not acute with iris bowing.
Painless; does not bow the iris forward.

steps.x: **D. Secondary angle-closure glaucoma from posterior synechiae.** Posterior synechiae carry a risk of secondary angle-closure glaucoma.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has a painful red right eye with photophobia. She has had a dry cough and breathlessness for 3 months and tender red lumps on both shins. Slit-lamp shows cells and flare. A chest X-ray is performed (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, typical of sarcoidosis.

questions.q: Which underlying condition is most likely?
questions.e: Uveitis, erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is sarcoidosis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which underlying condition is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: tender red lumps on both shins
steps.x: Erythema nodosum + cough + bilateral hilar nodes + uveitis = **sarcoidosis**.

elim: No inflammatory back pain; would not explain hilar nodes.
No oral or genital ulcers.
Can enlarge nodes but does not cause erythema nodosum with iritis typically.
Usually unilateral upper-zone disease with weight loss and night sweats.

steps.x: **D. Sarcoidosis.** Uveitis associations include sarcoidosis; check with a chest X-ray.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with a 5 year history of Crohn's disease has a painful, red left eye for 2 days. Bright light hurts and her vision is blurred. Redness is most intense around the cornea. The pupil is small. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 84 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Photophobia, ciliary flush, blurred vision and a small pupil in IBD is anterior uveitis; episcleritis is the classic distractor but is milder.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
IBD can cause both episcleritis and uveitis. **Photophobia + small pupil + ciliary flush** = uveitis.

elim: Itchy, bilateral, watering, no photophobia or small pupil.
Gritty discomfort with normal pupil.
Also IBD-linked, but mild and segmental without photophobia or a small pupil.
Fever, proptosis and painful eye movements with lid swelling.

steps.x: **B. Anterior uveitis.** Uveitis is associated with IBD; photophobia and a small pupil separate it from episcleritis.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with known posterior uveitis has had floaters in his left eye for 3 weeks. This morning he noticed flashing lights and a dark shadow spreading up from the lower part of his vision in that eye. Visual acuity is now hand movements.
questions.q: Which complication is most likely?
questions.e: Posterior uveitis carries a risk of retinal detachment, which presents with flashes and a spreading curtain or shadow.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which complication is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Flashes + **shadow/curtain** in posterior uveitis = **retinal detachment**.

elim: Painful photophobic red eye, not a spreading shadow.
Gradual blurring, no shadow or flashes.
Central blur in stressed young men, no curtain.
Bilateral, transient zigzag lines that resolve.

steps.x: **E. Retinal detachment.** Posterior uveitis risks retinal detachment: same-day referral.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man is told by the ophthalmologist that he has iritis. He asks what part of the eye is affected and whether it is related to the 'uvea' mentioned in his letter. He has no visual floaters and his fundus is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate description of his condition?
questions.e: The uvea is the iris, ciliary body and choroid; iritis is anterior uveitis, the commonest presentation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most accurate description of his condition? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Iritis = inflammation of the **iris**, the front of the uvea.

elim: That is conjunctivitis.
That is keratitis.
Retinitis; the uvea is iris, ciliary body and choroid.
A normal fundus and no floaters go against posterior disease.

steps.x: **A. Anterior uveitis affecting the iris.** Uvea = iris, ciliary body, choroid. Most uveitis is anterior (iritis).

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 1 day history of a painful red right eye with photophobia. Her GP suspects anterior uveitis and refers her to eye casualty. Her visual acuity is 6/9. She asks which test will confirm the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Uveitis is a clinical diagnosis made by ophthalmology; anterior uveitis is confirmed by cells and flare on slit-lamp examination.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Diagnosis is **clinical**: cells and flare at the slit lamp.

elim: Used when the fundus cannot be seen, not for anterior chamber cells.
Does not show anterior chamber cells.
Used for infective conjunctivitis.
Looks for an association; it does not make the diagnosis.

steps.x: **E. Slit-lamp examination.** Gold standard: clinical slit-lamp diagnosis by an ophthalmologist.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has a photophobic red left eye. On slit-lamp examination, the narrow beam shone through the anterior chamber shows white particles drifting in the aqueous and a hazy beam, like a torch in a smoky room. Intraocular pressure is 16 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding being described?
questions.e: Drifting inflammatory cells and a hazy beam from protein (flare) in the anterior chamber are the slit-lamp signs of anterior uveitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding being described? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: white particles drifting in the aqueous
steps.x: Particles = **cells**; hazy beam = **flare**.

elim: A corneal staining pattern in herpes simplex keratitis.
Blood layering in the anterior chamber after trauma.
A layered fluid level of pus, not drifting particles.
Deposits on the corneal endothelium, not particles drifting in aqueous.

steps.x: **A. Cells and flare.** Anterior uveitis: cells and flare in the anterior chamber.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has his third episode of acute anterior uveitis in 2 years. He has no other symptoms except stiffness in his lower back in the mornings that lasts an hour. His temperature is 36.7°C and BP 122/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation for an underlying cause?
o: HLA-B27, ESR/CRP and sacroiliac joint X-ray
questions.e: Recurrent uveitis or suspected systemic disease warrants HLA-B27, ESR/CRP and, with inflammatory back pain, a sacroiliac X-ray for ankylosing spondylitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation for an underlying cause? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: stiffness in his lower back in the mornings
steps.x: **Recurrent** iritis + inflammatory back pain = test for **AS**.

elim: SLE rarely presents with recurrent iritis and back stiffness.
Not indicated.
Used in multiple sclerosis-related uveitis only with neurology.
Recurrent disease warrants a search for a systemic cause.

steps.x: **B. HLA-B27, ESR/CRP and sacroiliac joint X-ray.** Recurrent uveitis: HLA-B27, ESR/CRP, sacroiliac X-ray, and chest X-ray for sarcoid.

questions.stem: A 38 year old Black woman has recurrent anterior uveitis in both eyes. She has had a dry cough for 2 months and feels tired. Her serum calcium is 2.78 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). HLA-B27 is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Recurrent uveitis with cough and hypercalcaemia suggests sarcoidosis, so a chest X-ray looking for hilar lymphadenopathy is next.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Uveitis + cough + **high calcium** = sarcoid = **chest X-ray**.

elim: No bowel symptoms.
No cardiac features.
No inflammatory back pain and HLA-B27 negative.
Giant cell arteritis does not cause uveitis in a 38 year old.

steps.x: **A. Chest X-ray.** Recurrent uveitis work-up includes a chest X-ray for sarcoidosis.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has a painful red right eye with photophobia and a small pupil. Her GP has no slit lamp. Vision is 6/12. The GP wonders whether any blood tests or imaging should be arranged before referral.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Arrange ESR and CRP and review in 1 week
questions.e: Uveitis is a clinical diagnosis made by ophthalmology and is treated as an emergency, so the patient needs same-day ophthalmology review.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Her GP has no slit lamp
steps.x: Suspected iritis = clinical diagnosis by **ophthalmology**, urgently.

elim: Delays an ophthalmological emergency.
Systemic work-up is second-line and should not delay review.
Second-line; does not make the diagnosis.
Not infective; delays treatment.

steps.x: **D. Same-day ophthalmology assessment.** Never delay referral for bloods in suspected uveitis.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has acute anterior uveitis confirmed on slit-lamp examination by the ophthalmologist. There is no corneal epithelial defect and intraocular pressure is 15 mmHg. He has severe photophobia and aching. He has no systemic symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: First-line treatment is a topical corticosteroid (prednisolone acetate 1%) plus a cycloplegic/mydriatic such as cyclopentolate.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Iritis: **steroid drop** to treat inflammation + **cycloplegic** for pain and synechiae.

elim: For herpetic disease, not idiopathic iritis.
Systemic steroid is for severe disease.
Constricts the pupil, worsening synechiae and spasm.
Not infective.

steps.x: **E. Topical prednisolone acetate 1% and cyclopentolate.** First line: topical steroid plus cycloplegic (cyclopentolate or atropine).

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman visits a walk-in centre with a 1 day history of a painful red left eye. She cannot tolerate bright lights and the redness is greatest around the cornea. The left pupil is small and irregular. She had a similar episode 2 years ago.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Advise sunglasses and review in 2 weeks
Start topical steroid drops in the walk-in centre
questions.e: Uveitis is treated as an ophthalmological emergency; the first step is urgent referral to ophthalmology.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: redness is greatest around the cornea
steps.x: Probable iritis outside eye services = **refer urgently**.

elim: Uveitis is an ophthalmological emergency.
Does not treat iritis.
Not infective.
Steroids should be started by ophthalmology after excluding infection at the slit lamp.

steps.x: **E. Urgent same-day referral to ophthalmology.** First line in uveitis: urgent ophthalmology referral.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with sarcoidosis has severe anterior uveitis in both eyes with dense cells and a fibrinous reaction. Despite 2 weeks of hourly prednisolone acetate 1% drops and cyclopentolate, her vision has fallen to 6/24 in both eyes.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Severe uveitis not controlled by topical therapy needs a systemic corticosteroid such as oral prednisolone.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: severe anterior uveitis in both eyes
steps.x: Severe, failing topical treatment = **systemic steroid**.

elim: No infection.
Treats angle closure, not inflammation.
Disease is worsening.
Too weak for severe uveitis.

steps.x: **C. Oral prednisolone.** Second line in severe uveitis: oral prednisolone.

questions.stem: A 32 year old man with Behçet's disease has a 4 day history of rapidly falling vision in both eyes. He has new oral ulcers and painful red nodules on his shins. Fundoscopy shows bilateral retinal vasculitis with haemorrhages. Visual acuity is 6/36 in both eyes.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Bilateral uveitis with severe systemic disease such as Behçet's is an emergency needing high-dose systemic corticosteroid started urgently.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Bilateral, sight-threatening, systemic = **urgent high-dose systemic steroid**.

elim: Used for diabetic retinopathy, not inflammation.
Helps mucocutaneous Behçet's but not sight-threatening uveitis.
Does not control posterior or bilateral disease.
Does not reach posterior disease and is inadequate for bilateral sight-threatening disease.

steps.x: **A. High-dose systemic corticosteroid.** Behçet's bilateral uveitis: urgent high-dose systemic corticosteroid.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has had five flares of anterior uveitis in 18 months, each needing oral prednisolone. Flares return when prednisolone is reduced below 10 mg. She has developed raised intraocular pressure and early cataract. She has an underlying autoimmune disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: Recurrent or autoimmune uveitis is managed long-term with specialist-led immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or azathioprine, sparing steroids.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate long-term management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: raised intraocular pressure and early cataract
steps.x: Steroid-dependent, with steroid complications = **steroid-sparing immunosuppressant**.

elim: Steroid side effects are already causing cataract and raised IOP.
Not infective.
Does not control inflammation.
Treats a complication, not the recurrent disease.

steps.x: **B. Methotrexate under specialist care.** Long-term: methotrexate or azathioprine under specialist care.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man with acute iritis is started on prednisolone acetate 1% drops by the ophthalmologist. He still has intense aching in the eye and the pupil is small, with early adhesions forming at the pupil margin. Intraocular pressure is 14 mmHg.
questions.q: Which drug should be added?
questions.e: A cycloplegic/mydriatic (cyclopentolate or atropine) relieves ciliary spasm and dilates the pupil, reducing pain and breaking early synechiae.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which drug should be added? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: early adhesions forming at the pupil margin
steps.x: Aching = ciliary spasm; adhesions = synechiae. Both need a **cycloplegic**.

elim: Lowers IOP, which is normal; prostaglandins can worsen inflammation.
Lowers IOP, which is normal.
Constricts the pupil, encouraging synechiae and spasm.
Lowers IOP, which is normal.

steps.x: **A. Cyclopentolate eye drops.** Steroid + cycloplegic is first line in anterior uveitis.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman has posterior uveitis in her right eye with vitritis and patches of choroiditis. Vision has fallen to 6/36 over 10 days. Infection has been excluded by the ophthalmologist. Her BP is 128/82 mmHg and glucose is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Severe or posterior uveitis needs systemic corticosteroid, as topical drops do not reach the posterior segment.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Severe sight-threatening posterior disease = **systemic** steroid.

elim: Infection has been excluded.
Treats retinal ischaemia, not inflammation.
Does not treat posterior inflammation.
Drops do not reach the choroid in therapeutic levels.

steps.x: **B. Oral prednisolone.** Severe uveitis: oral prednisolone.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has his first attack of acute anterior uveitis. He is HLA-B27 positive. He asks why his back disease and his eye disease are linked.
questions.q: Which best explains the link?
o: Direct bacterial spread from the spine
Immune complex deposition from back inflammation
Shared genetic predisposition to T-cell mediated inflammation
Side effect of NSAIDs for his back
Spinal cord compression affecting the eye
questions.e: HLA-B27 reflects a shared genetic predisposition causing T-cell mediated autoimmune inflammation of both the spine and the anterior uvea.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best explains the link? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
HLA-B27 = MHC class I = presents to **T cells**; same predisposition in eye and spine.

elim: Not infective.
Not the mechanism in HLA-B27 disease.
NSAIDs do not cause uveitis.
No neurological link.

steps.x: **C. Shared genetic predisposition to T-cell mediated inflammation.** HLA-B27 uveitis: shared genetics, T-cell mediated inflammation.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with anterior uveitis is shown her slit-lamp image. The light beam is visible as it crosses the normally clear aqueous, and white cells are floating in it. She asks why the fluid has become cloudy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: Inflammation breaks down the blood-aqueous barrier so protein (flare) and inflammatory cells leak into the aqueous humour.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Protein in aqueous = **flare**; it comes from leaky vessels = barrier breakdown.

elim: Would give hyphaema or rubeosis, not flare.
Does not cause protein leak.
Not the cause of flare in iritis.
Gives pigment dispersion, not cells and flare.

steps.x: **B. Breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier.** Cells and flare: blood-aqueous barrier breakdown.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man is given atropine drops for anterior uveitis. He notices his vision is blurred for close work and his pupil is large, but his deep aching pain has improved within a day.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pain relief?
o: Paralysis of the ciliary muscle and iris sphincter
questions.e: Cycloplegics block muscarinic receptors to paralyse the ciliary muscle and iris sphincter, relieving ciliary spasm and reducing synechiae risk.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pain relief? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Loss of accommodation + big pupil = ciliary muscle and sphincter paralysed.

elim: Atropine dilates the pupil.
Atropine is not anti-inflammatory; the steroid treats inflammation.
That is how timolol and acetazolamide act.
Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors.

steps.x: **C. Paralysis of the ciliary muscle and iris sphincter.** Cycloplegics relieve ciliary spasm and prevent synechiae.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has had chronic anterior uveitis for 8 years, treated with frequent courses of steroid drops. At review his vision is 6/12, the eye is quiet and intraocular pressure is 30 mmHg (10–21). The optic disc cup is enlarging.
questions.q: Which best explains his raised intraocular pressure?
questions.e: Chronic inflammation (trabecular damage) and long-term steroid use both raise intraocular pressure and cause glaucoma, as well as cataract.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which best explains his raised intraocular pressure? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Long-standing uveitis + years of steroids = **raised IOP**.

elim: He is pain-free with a quiet eye.
Presents in infancy.
No diabetes or rubeosis.
Usually lowers rather than raises IOP.

steps.x: **B. Chronic inflammation and steroid use.** Chronic uveitis and steroids: cataract and raised IOP.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with acute iritis stops her cyclopentolate drops after one day because they blur her reading. Two weeks later her pupil is irregular and does not dilate fully, and the iris margin is stuck to the lens surface in several places.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her pupil abnormality?
o: Inflamed iris adhering to the anterior lens capsule
questions.e: Without cycloplegia, the inflamed iris sticks to the anterior lens capsule (posterior synechiae), giving an irregular pupil and risk of secondary angle closure.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her pupil abnormality? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Small inflamed pupil left constricted = iris glues to the **lens** = posterior synechiae.

elim: Gives ptosis and a down-and-out eye.
Gives sectoral atrophy, not adhesion.
Does not change pupil shape.
Horner's: small regular pupil with ptosis.

steps.x: **B. Inflamed iris adhering to the anterior lens capsule.** Cycloplegics prevent posterior synechiae.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked which structures can be inflamed in a patient described as having panuveitis. The patient has photophobia, cells in the anterior chamber, vitreous haze and patches of choroiditis.
questions.q: Which structures make up the uvea?
questions.e: The uvea is the iris, ciliary body and choroid; inflammation of all parts is panuveitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which structures make up the uvea? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Front (iris), middle (ciliary body), back (choroid).

elim: Outer coat and surface, not uvea.
Not uveal tissues.
Lens and retina are not uvea.
Neural tissues, not uvea.

steps.x: **C. Iris, ciliary body and choroid.** Uvea = iris + ciliary body + choroid.
